activities.caption: pair the BioBrick vocabulary with its meaning
activities.name: synBrickMatch

config.prompt: The founding artefact and its honest physics — pair them:

pairs.left: promoters, ribosome-binding sites, coding sequences, terminators
standard prefixes and suffixes flanking every part
student teams assembling cells from catalogued parts
pairs.right: iGEM — the field's training pipeline since 2004

pairs.left: a promoter's strength shifts with neighbours, growth phase and copy number
pairs.right: context-dependence — the leakiness no resistor has

config.why: The abstraction hierarchy (parts → devices → systems) is borrowed from electronics; 'characterised part' means characterised in specified conditions — the field's central argument is how much context can be tamed.

config.prompt: Engineering's quantitative habits, imported — put the flow in order:
items: Simulate to see what the model predicts
Choose parameters: promoter strengths, degradation tags
Build — insert the wired-together regulatory elements
Reconcile: the measurement shows where the model lied
config.why: Modelling guides; reality teaches — the loop that took the 2000 toggle switch and repressilator from noisy proofs of concept to counters, logic gates, edge detection and kill-switches.

activities.anchor: the smallest genome known to run
activities.caption: call the magnitude — minimal life's parts count
activities.name: synGenesEstimate

config.prompt: The 2016 syn3.0 bacterium runs on the smallest genome known. Roughly how many genes does it carry?
config.why: 473 genes — and about a third of them could not be explained. Every gene in a minimal genome is necessary, so every one is a research question.
config.context: Its 2010 ancestor syn1.0 carried watermark sequences — the first typographical marks in a living thing.

activities.anchor: engineered yeast by the Keasling group
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the products ledger
activities.name: synShippedSpot

config.prompt: This what-has-shipped answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Recombinant insulin has been made in engineered bacteria since 1982.
Artemisinic acid, the antimalarial precursor, was brewed in engineered yeast after a decade of work.
CAR-T therapies reprogramme patient immune cells to hunt cancer.
The mRNA vaccines succeeded because each was a bespoke build from scratch, months of bench work per dose.
CRISPR paper diagnostics (SHERLOCK/DETECTR) detect a sequence with attomolar sensitivity.
config.correction: The mRNA vaccines ran on platform thinking — design the sequence, synthesise to order — which is exactly what delivered them at pandemic speed.
config.why: The pattern in the successes: each shipped product needed years of unglamorous optimisation after the elegant design — but the platform logic, not bespoke builds, is what scaled.

activities.anchor: assembled a cell from non-living components
activities.caption: writing a genome vs creating life — drag between them
activities.name: synLifeCompare

config.prompt: The misconception's two poles — drag the divider:

before.label: writing a genome
before.text: 2010: a chemically synthesised genome booted up — inside a recipient bacterial cell whose cytoplasm did the booting.

after.label: creating life
after.text: Nobody has assembled a cell from non-living components. The gap between the two panels is the entire origin-of-life problem, still open.

config.why: The field's most aggressive work rewires or minimises existing life — engineering's borrowings from biology, not biology's replacement.

activities.caption: choose the lab's brakes — a dual-use run
activities.name: synBrakesBranch

config.root: You lead a synthetic-biology lab: print-order DNA shipping daily, engineered organisms on the bench. Dual-use is structural, so the brakes are yours to engineer.

start.text: Which brake do you build first?

choices.label: Engineer an auxotrophic chassis
choices.feedback: Containment by design: it dies outside supplemented media.

choices.label: Screen every DNA order against dangerous-sequence databases
choices.feedback: The synthesis companies' IGSC protocols — upstream, by consent.

choices.label: Release a gene drive against malaria mosquitoes now
choices.feedback: No natural precedent — and neighbours who never consented.

auxo.text: Kill-switches and firewall plasmids complete the kit, layered over BSL physical controls.

screen.text: A rare case of industry adopting upstream censorship-by-consent — with publication policies like the H5N1 controversy's template (2011–12).

drive.text: The field's own researchers demand community consent and staged testing before any release: the governance gap is the research programme.

config.why: Capability arrived before consensus: the 2018 CRISPR-babies conviction set the line — somatic therapy increasingly approved, heritable editing banned nearly everywhere — and the brakes are being engineered in real time.

activities.caption: file the outcomes — on-target or off
activities.name: synPrecisionBuckets

config.prompt: Precision is a distribution. File each outcome:

items.label: the guide pairs at the designed 20-base target
Cas cuts a sequence carrying a few mismatches elsewhere
the cell's error-prone repair scrambles the intended site
whole-genome sequencing of edited cells finds unbidden edits
the designed cut lands at the intended locus
a mosaic embryo — different cells carrying different outcomes

config.why: Repair of a targeted cut is the cell's own error-prone machinery — so precision is a measured, distributional property, never a guarantee; one reason germline editing is categorically different from somatic therapy.

activities.caption: true or false — the regulatory map
activities.name: synGovJudge

statements.s: US regulation sorts engineered organisms by product; EU regulation sorts by process.
statements.why: USDA/EPA/FDA by product; the EU process-based — both designed for 1980s transgenics and recombinant drugs.

statements.s: Gene drives have natural precedent in wild populations.
statements.why: Engineered to spread through wild populations with no natural precedent — they sit in a governance gap.

statements.s: Environmental release of a gene drive affects neighbours who never consented.
statements.why: Which is why researchers themselves publish frameworks demanding consent and staged testing.

statements.s: GMO frameworks already cover gene synthesis, CRISPR and gene drives.
statements.why: They predate all three — the gap is the live research programme.
